title: CC (2026 outline) practice exam
note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from ISC2's public CC exam outline (effective Sep 1, 2026). Not real exam questions. The real CC is adaptive (100-125 questions); this is a fixed 100-question stand-in.

q.q: A hospital's patient portal goes down for six hours during a ransomware attack, but no records are stolen or changed. Which part of the CIA triad was MOST affected?
o: Availability
Right. Patients and staff couldn't reach the data when they needed it. Nothing was read or altered.
Confidentiality
Confidentiality is about who can see the data. The scenario says nothing was stolen.
Integrity
Integrity is about unauthorized changes. The records weren't altered.
Non-repudiation
Non-repudiation proves who did an action. The problem here is that nobody could use the system.

q.q: A user logs in with a password and a code from an app, opens the payroll folder, and the system writes each file she opens to a log. Which step is ACCOUNTING?
o: Writing each file she opens to a log
Right. Accounting records what an identity did, so it can be reviewed later.
Checking the password and the app code
That's authentication: proving she is who she says she is.
Deciding she may open the payroll folder
That's authorization: what an authenticated user is allowed to do.
Giving her a username when she was hired
That's identification and provisioning, which happen before any of the AAA steps.

q.q: An attacker slips fake records into the data used to train a fraud-detection model, so the model learns to ignore a certain kind of fraud. Which security goal did the attack target FIRST?
o: Integrity of the training data
Right. Poisoning changes the data without permission, and the model then learns the wrong lesson.
Confidentiality of the model's settings
Nothing was stolen or read. The attacker added data instead.
Availability of the fraud-detection service
The model keeps running. It just gives wrong answers.
Privacy of the customers in the data set
Customer data wasn't exposed. The data was tampered with.

q.q: A company wants proof that a customer, and not someone else, approved a contract sent through its website. Which control gives the strongest non-repudiation?
o: The customer signs the contract with their own private key
Right. Only the key holder can create that signature, so the customer can't credibly deny it.
The website sends the contract over HTTPS
HTTPS protects the contract in transit. It doesn't prove who approved it.
The contract is stored on an encrypted drive
Encryption at rest protects confidentiality, not proof of who signed.
The server stores a SHA-256 hash of the signed contract file
A hash shows the file hasn't changed, but anyone can make one. It isn't tied to the customer.

q.q: A marketing team wants to load customer names, emails and purchase history into a public AI chatbot to write campaigns. Which principle is the BIGGEST concern?
o: Privacy of the customers' personal data
Right. Personal data sent to an outside AI service may be stored or used for training, outside the company's control.
Availability of the chatbot during the campaign
A busy chatbot is an inconvenience. Leaking personal data is the real risk.
Integrity of the campaign wording the chatbot writes
Bad wording can be fixed by an editor. Personal data can't be pulled back once shared.
Authentication of the team members to the chatbot
Logging in doesn't stop the data from leaving the company.

q.q: Which example BEST shows authorization rather than authentication?
o: A help desk technician can reset passwords but can't open the HR share
Right. Authorization decides what an already-identified user may do.
A technician enters a PIN and taps a badge at the door
That's authentication: proving identity with two factors.
The system asks for a fingerprint before it unlocks the laptop for the user
A fingerprint is a way to authenticate, not a decision about permissions.
A login page checks a password against the stored hash
Checking a password proves identity. It's authentication.

q.q: A risk assessment finds that a server holding public brochures has a known flaw. Patching would take a week of downtime, and the data is public anyway. Leadership signs off and documents the decision. Which risk response is this?
o: Acceptance
Right. Leadership knowingly keeps the risk because its impact is low, and documents that choice.
Avoidance
Avoidance stops the activity that creates the risk. The server is still running.
Mitigation
Mitigation adds a control to lower the risk. No control was added.
Transference
Transference shifts the cost to someone else, like an insurer. That didn't happen.

q.q: In the risk management life cycle, what should happen right AFTER an organization identifies its risks?
o: Assess each risk's likelihood and impact
Right. You have to rate each risk before you can decide which ones to treat first.
Buy insurance for the most expensive assets
Insurance is one way to treat a risk, and it comes after assessment.
Install controls on every system at once
Treating everything before rating it wastes money on low risks.
Write the lessons-learned report
Lessons learned belongs to incident response, not the start of risk management.

q.q: A small business buys cyber insurance that pays for recovery costs after a data breach. Which risk response did it choose?
o: Transference
Right. Part of the financial impact moves to the insurer.
Mitigation
Insurance doesn't make a breach less likely. It moves the cost.
Acceptance
Paying for insurance is an action. Acceptance means doing nothing more.
Avoidance
The business still stores the data, so the risk still exists.

q.q: Two risks score the same on likelihood. Risk A would expose 50 records; Risk B would stop the payment system for a day. Using impact to set priority, which is MOST important to know before ranking them?
o: What each outcome would cost the organization
Right. Priority comes from likelihood times impact, so you need the impact of each outcome in the same terms.
Which of the two risks the assessment team found first
The order you found risks in doesn't change how much they matter.
Which team owns the server
Ownership matters for treatment, not for ranking the risk.
How many controls each system already has
Existing controls feed into likelihood, which is already equal here.

q.q: A team writes down a risk, its owner, its score and the chosen response, and reviews the list every quarter. What is this list called?
o: A risk register
Right. The register tracks each risk, who owns it and how it's handled over time.
A business impact analysis
A BIA ranks business processes by how much an outage hurts. It's an input, not the tracking list.
An acceptable use policy
An AUP tells users how they may use systems.
A change request
A change request asks permission to change a system.

q.q: A company adds email filtering and staff training to cut the chance of a phishing breach. Some risk is still left afterward. What is the leftover risk called?
o: Residual risk
Right. Residual risk is what remains after controls are applied.
Inherent risk
Inherent risk is the level before any controls.
Risk appetite
Risk appetite is how much risk leadership is willing to take, not the leftover amount.
Transferred risk
No risk was moved to a third party here.

q.q: Which document is MANDATORY and states a specific requirement, such as "all laptops must use AES-256 full-disk encryption"?
o: A standard
Right. Standards set specific, required ways to meet a policy.
A guideline
Guidelines are recommendations. They're optional.
A policy
Policies give high-level intent, like "protect company data", not the exact setting.
A procedure
Procedures give the step-by-step how-to for a task.

q.q: Where do security policies, standards and procedures usually come from?
o: Laws and regulations, then the organization's own policies, then standards and procedures
Right. Outside requirements shape policy, and policy is carried out by standards and procedures.
From procedures first, which are rolled up into policies once they have been proven to work
Governance flows from the top down, not from day-to-day steps up.
Vendor manuals, which set the policy for each product
Vendor manuals can feed procedures, but they don't set the organization's policy.
The help desk, which writes the rules users must follow
The help desk follows procedures. Leadership approves policy.

q.q: A U.S. hospital handles patient health records. Which requirement is it legally bound by, not just encouraged to follow?
o: HIPAA
Right. HIPAA is a U.S. law that protects health information.
The NIST Cybersecurity Framework
NIST CSF is a voluntary framework for most private organizations.
ISO/IEC 27001
ISO 27001 is a standard organizations may choose to certify against.
The CIS Critical Security Controls
CIS Controls are a recommended set of best practices, not a law.

q.q: A new employee needs to know the exact clicks to request VPN access. Which document should she read?
o: A procedure
Right. Procedures give step-by-step instructions for a task.
A policy
Policy says why remote access must be controlled, not how to request it.
A standard
A standard sets required settings, like which VPN protocol to use.
A baseline report
A baseline describes a secure starting configuration, not the request steps.

q.q: An organization wants a recognized framework to organize its security program around Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. Which one fits?
o: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0
Right. CSF 2.0 is built around those six functions.
PCI DSS
PCI DSS is a standard for protecting payment card data.
GDPR
GDPR is an EU privacy regulation, not a program framework.
The OWASP Top 10 list of web application risks
The OWASP Top 10 lists common web application risks.

q.q: Before rolling out an AI writing tool, a company writes a short document saying staff must not paste confidential data into it. What type of document is this?
o: A policy
Right. It states management's rule for acceptable use of the tool.
A guideline
"Must not" makes it a requirement. Guidelines are suggestions.
A procedure
It doesn't list steps for doing a task.
A regulation
Regulations come from governments, not from the company itself.

q.q: Which of these is an ADMINISTRATIVE control?
o: A required background check before hiring
Right. Administrative (managerial) controls are policies, processes and people practices.
A firewall rule that blocks Telnet
Firewall rules are technical (logical) controls.
A badge reader installed on the server room door
Badge readers are physical controls.
Disk encryption on every laptop
Encryption is a technical control.

q.q: A data center adds bollards outside the entrance, a mantrap and security guards. Which type of control are these?
o: Physical
Right. They protect the building and the people and equipment inside it.
Technical
Technical controls are enforced by hardware and software settings, like ACLs.
Administrative
Administrative controls are policies and procedures.
Corrective
Corrective controls fix damage after an event. These stop it.

q.q: A security camera is installed in a hallway with a sign that says "This area is monitored." Besides recording, what is the sign's MAIN purpose?
o: To deter people from trying anything
Right. Visible warnings discourage an attack before it starts.
To correct damage after an incident
Corrective controls restore systems, like backups.
To compensate for a missing door lock
A compensating control replaces a control you can't use. The sign doesn't replace a lock.
To authenticate people walking by
A camera and sign don't prove anyone's identity.

q.q: An old factory machine can't be patched. The team puts it on its own network segment and blocks all internet traffic to it. What kind of control is the segment?
o: A compensating control
Right. It lowers the risk when the normal control, patching, isn't possible.
A deterrent control
Nothing here warns or discourages an attacker.
An administrative control
A network segment is enforced by equipment, not by policy alone.
A directive control
Directive controls tell people what to do, like a policy.

q.q: A company lets staff use an AI coding assistant. Which pair is a TECHNICAL and an ADMINISTRATIVE control for it, in that order?
o: Blocking uploads of source code to unapproved AI sites; a rule that staff review AI code before merging
Right. The block is enforced by software; the review rule is a policy people follow.
A rule that staff review all AI-written code; a web filter that blocks unapproved AI sites
The order is reversed: the rule is administrative and the filter is technical.
Locking the server room; annual security training
A lock is physical, not technical.
Annual security training; a sign about AI use in the break room
Both of these are administrative or directive. Neither is technical.

q.q: Which control is BEST at detecting, rather than preventing, an intruder on the network?
o: An IDS that alerts on suspicious traffic
Right. An IDS watches and alerts. It doesn't block on its own.
A firewall that drops all inbound traffic from unknown sources
Dropping traffic prevents it.
Strong password rules
Password rules make guessing harder, which is prevention.
Full-disk encryption
Encryption prevents data from being read if a device is stolen.

q.q: Under the ISC2 Code of Ethics, which canon comes FIRST?
o: Protect society, the common good, necessary public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure
Right. The canons are in priority order, and duty to society comes first.
Provide diligent and competent service to your principals and clients
That canon is third, after society and acting honorably.
Advance and protect the profession
That's the fourth canon.
Follow every instruction from your employer
This isn't a canon. Duty to principals comes after society and honesty.

q.q: A company reads a vendor's audit reports and checks references before signing a cloud contract. Which concept does this show?
o: Due diligence
Right. Due diligence is researching and verifying before you act.
Due care
Due care is acting responsibly once you're in the relationship, like applying the controls you promised.
Risk transference
Signing a contract can transfer some risk, but checking the vendor first is diligence.
Separation of duties
SoD splits tasks between people to prevent fraud.

q.q: After moving to the cloud, a company keeps patching its virtual machines and reviewing access every month, as its policy requires. Which concept does this show?
o: Due care
Right. Due care is doing what a reasonable organization should do to protect its assets, day after day.
Due diligence
Due diligence is the research done before a decision.
Risk avoidance
The company still runs the systems, so it hasn't avoided the risk.
Non-repudiation
Non-repudiation is about proving who performed an action.

q.q: A friend at another company asks you to look up his ex-partner's address in your employer's customer database. What should you do?
o: Refuse, because it misuses access and harms someone's privacy
Right. Using access for personal reasons breaks the canons about acting honorably and protecting the public.
Look it up only if he promises not to share it with anyone else
A promise doesn't make misusing access acceptable.
Ask your manager for permission first
No manager can approve misusing customer data for a personal favor.
Give the city but not the street address
Any part of the record is still misuse of customer data.

q.q: You discover that an AI hiring tool your company uses rejects most applicants over 50. What is the MOST ethical first step?
o: Report it to the tool's owners for review
Right. Acting honorably includes raising unfair outcomes, and the owners need to investigate.
Post the finding on social media so job seekers are warned in time
Going public first skips the proper channel and may break your duty to your employer.
Quietly change the tool's settings yourself
Making unapproved changes isn't your call and could break other things.
Ignore it because the tool came from a vendor
Using a vendor's tool doesn't remove your company's responsibility.

q.q: A pentest client asks you to also test a partner's servers that aren't in your signed scope, "since you're already in there." What should you do?
o: Decline until the partner gives written permission
Right. Testing systems without the owner's authorization is illegal and unethical, whatever the client wants.
Test them quietly and only report serious findings
Quietly testing without permission is still unauthorized access.
Test them, because your client approved it
Your client can't authorize testing systems it doesn't own.
Run only passive scans, since those don't count
Scanning someone else's systems without permission is still out of scope.

q.q: What is the MAIN purpose of a governance, risk and compliance (GRC) program?
o: To line up security decisions with business goals, risk limits and legal duties
Right. GRC ties governance, risk management and compliance together so they support the mission.
To replace the incident response team with automated tools
GRC sets direction and oversight. It doesn't replace responders.
To make sure every single system passes a monthly vulnerability scan
Scanning is one control. GRC is the program that decides which controls matter and why.
To give auditors full admin access to every system
Auditors need evidence, not admin rights. GRC doesn't hand out access.

q.q: An auditor asks a company to prove it meets a regulation's logging rule. What does the company need MOST?
o: Evidence, like log settings, mapped to the rule
Right. Compliance is shown with evidence tied to each requirement.
A new firewall from a well-known vendor
Buying equipment doesn't prove anything to an auditor.
A signed statement from the IT manager that logging is turned on
An auditor needs proof, not a verbal assurance.
A penetration test of the website
A pentest doesn't show that the logging rule is met.

q.q: Which group should own and approve an organization's overall security risk decisions?
o: Senior leadership
Right. Leaders own the mission, so they set risk appetite and accept risk on its behalf.
The help desk
The help desk carries out procedures. It doesn't own business risk.
An outside penetration tester
A tester finds issues. The organization decides what to do about them.
Each employee for their own laptop
Individuals follow policy, but they can't accept risk for the organization.

q.q: A company uses one platform to track policies, the risk register, audit findings and control evidence. What kind of tool is this?
o: A GRC tool
Right. GRC platforms keep governance, risk and compliance records in one place.
A SIEM
A SIEM collects and correlates security logs.
An EDR agent
EDR watches endpoints for malicious behavior.
A password manager
A password manager stores credentials.

q.q: Why does compliance alone NOT guarantee that an organization is secure?
o: A regulation sets a minimum, and threats can still get past it
Right. Meeting a checklist doesn't cover every risk the organization actually faces.
Compliance rules only apply to companies with more than 1,000 staff
Compliance duties depend on the law and the data, not just company size.
Auditors aren't allowed to look at technical controls
Auditors regularly review technical controls.
Compliance reports are always written by the vendor
The organization produces its own evidence.

q.q: A new rule requires the company to label every AI-generated customer email. Which part of GRC deals with this FIRST?
o: Compliance: finding out what the rule requires and showing it's met
Right. Compliance tracks outside requirements and proves the organization follows them.
Incident response: treating each AI email as an incident
An email that needs a label isn't a security incident.
Disaster recovery: backing up every AI-written email to an offsite location
Backups don't satisfy a labeling requirement.
Penetration testing: testing the email server
A pentest doesn't tell you whether emails are labeled.

q.q: A flood closes a company's main office. Staff work from a second office and keep taking customer orders. Which plan made that possible?
o: The business continuity plan
Right. BC keeps critical business functions running during a disruption.
The incident response plan
IR handles security incidents like malware, not keeping the business running through a flood.
The change management plan
Change management controls planned changes to systems.
The acceptable use policy for staff
The AUP sets rules for using company systems.

q.q: After a fire, the IT team rebuilds servers at a backup site and restores data from last night's backups. Which plan are they following?
o: The disaster recovery plan
Right. DR restores IT systems and data after a disaster.
The business impact analysis
The BIA is an earlier analysis that ranks which processes matter most.
The data classification policy
Classification labels data by sensitivity.
The security awareness plan
Awareness trains people. It doesn't restore servers.

q.q: A business can lose at most 4 hours of order data. Which value describes this?
o: Recovery point objective (RPO)
Right. RPO is how much data, measured in time, you can afford to lose.
Recovery time objective (RTO)
RTO is how fast the system must be back up.
Mean time between failures (MTBF)
MTBF predicts how often a part fails.
Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD)
MTD is the longest a process can be down before the damage is too great, not the data lost.

q.q: A retailer's checkout system must be running again within 2 hours of an outage. Which value is this?
o: Recovery time objective (RTO)
Right. RTO is the target time to restore the system.
Recovery point objective (RPO)
RPO measures data loss, not restore time.
Service level of the internet provider
The ISP's SLA covers the ISP, not the retailer's own recovery target.
Mean time to detect (MTTD)
MTTD measures how quickly an issue is noticed.

q.q: A company backs up its customer database every night but has never tried a restore. What is the BIGGEST risk?
o: The backups may not work when they're needed
Right. An untested backup is a guess. Regular restore tests prove recovery works.
The backups use too much storage
Storage cost is a minor issue compared with failing to recover.
Restores might break the change process
Restore tests can be planned and approved like any change.
Attackers can read backups more easily than live data
That depends on how backups are protected. The bigger gap here is no testing.

q.q: A company's support chatbot runs on an AI model. Which item should its disaster recovery plan back up IN ADDITION to the usual servers and databases?
o: The model's settings and the data sets used to build it
Right. Without them you can't rebuild the same AI service after a disaster.
The chat window's color scheme
Styling is easy to recreate and isn't what keeps the service working.
Every customer's browser history
The company doesn't hold that, and shouldn't.
A list of the AI vendors the team considered before choosing one
Old vendor research doesn't help restore the service.

q.q: Which factor does MOST to build a strong security culture?
o: Leaders who visibly follow the rules themselves
Right. People copy what leaders do. Visible support from the top shapes the culture.
A long annual training video everyone must click through
One yearly video rarely changes behavior.
Punishing anyone who reports a mistake
Punishment makes people hide mistakes, which hurts security.
Letting IT handle security so nobody else has to think about it
Security depends on everyone, not only IT.

q.q: An employee gets a call from "IT support" asking for her MFA code to "fix her account." What kind of attack is this?
o: Vishing
Right. It's social engineering over the phone to steal a login code.
Smishing
Smishing uses text messages.
Tailgating
Tailgating is following someone through a secure door.
Whaling (targets executives)
Whaling targets senior executives.

q.q: A finance clerk gets an email that looks like it's from the CEO, asking for an urgent wire transfer before the end of the day. What should the clerk do FIRST?
o: Confirm the request with the CEO using a known phone number
Right. Verifying through a separate, trusted channel stops business email compromise.
Reply to the email and ask if it's real
Replying goes back to the attacker if the email is fake.
Send the wire, since the CEO said it's urgent
Urgency is a classic social engineering pressure tactic.
Forward the email to the whole finance team so they can weigh in
That spreads the phishing email instead of verifying it.

q.q: Attackers now use AI to write phishing emails with perfect grammar in the target's own style. How should awareness training change?
o: Teach staff to judge the request, not the spelling
Right. Spelling and grammar errors are no longer reliable warning signs.
Stop training, because the emails can't be spotted anymore
People can still spot odd requests, urgency and changed payment details.
Tell staff to ignore all external emails
That would stop normal business.
Focus only on spotting bad grammar
AI removes exactly that clue.

q.q: Which password habit should awareness training encourage?
o: Use a long, unique passphrase for each account, kept in a password manager
Right. Length and uniqueness stop guessing and password reuse.
Change a short, complex password every two weeks
Frequent changes to short passwords lead to weak, predictable patterns.
Use the same strong password everywhere so it's easy to remember
One breach would then expose every account.
Write passwords on a sticky note under the keyboard
Anyone at the desk could read it.

q.q: After a phishing simulation, 12% of staff clicked the link. What is the BEST next step?
o: Give short, targeted training to those who clicked and run another test later
Right. Simulations are for learning, and retesting shows whether it worked.
Fire everyone who clicked
Punishment discourages reporting and doesn't build skills.
Stop running simulations because they upset and embarrass staff
Simulations are one of the best ways to measure awareness.
Block all links in all emails
That breaks normal work. Training and filtering together work better.

q.q: Which is a KEY RISK INDICATOR (KRI) rather than a simple activity count?
o: Percent of critical servers with patches 30+ days late
Right. A KRI warns that risk is rising before something bad happens.
The number of security training videos posted to the portal this month
That counts activity. It doesn't show whether risk is rising.
The number of firewalls the company owns
Owning equipment says nothing about risk.
How many emails the mail server sent today
Email volume isn't a risk measure.

q.q: A CISO needs to show the board, in five minutes, whether security is getting better. Which format is BEST?
o: A short dashboard of a few trends against targets
Right. Leaders need a quick view of direction and of where the targets are missed.
The full SIEM log export for the quarter, sorted by date
Raw logs are far too detailed for a board.
A list of every firewall rule
Rule lists are technical detail, not a measure of improvement.
The source code of the security tools
Code doesn't tell the board anything about risk.

q.q: Mean time to respond (MTTR) to incidents went from 9 hours to 3 hours over six months. What does this metric tell leadership?
o: The team is containing incidents faster
Right. Lower MTTR means less time for attackers to cause damage.
There are fewer attacks against the company than before
MTTR measures speed, not the number of attacks.
Every system is now fully patched
Response time doesn't show patch status.
The company can now skip backups
Faster response doesn't replace recovery capability.

q.q: A security team sees that alerts from its AI-based email filter that turn out to be false alarms jumped from 2% to 20%. Why is this worth putting on a dashboard?
o: It's a warning sign that the model may have drifted and needs review
Right. A sudden change in how a model behaves is a useful AI-related risk indicator.
It proves the filter is now catching far more real attacks than before
More false alarms means more mistakes, not more real catches.
It shows the email server needs more storage
False alarm rates don't measure storage.
It means staff no longer need awareness training
Filter mistakes don't change the need for training.

q.q: A scorecard shows 99% of laptops have encryption turned on, but it was built from a list that leaves out 200 contractor laptops. What is the MAIN problem?
o: The metric is misleading because the data behind it is incomplete
Right. A metric is only as good as its data. Missing devices hide real risk.
A figure of 99% is too high for any real company to believe
High numbers can be real. The issue is what's missing.
Scorecards should never show percentages
Percentages are common and useful when the data is complete.
Contractor laptops don't need encryption
Contractor devices can hold company data too.

q.q: A new analyst starts Monday. What should happen FIRST in the identity life cycle?
o: An account is provisioned with her role's access
Right. Provisioning gives access based on a defined, approved role.
She gets the same access as the coworker who sits next to her desk
Copying a coworker's access often gives too much. Access should follow her role.
She gets admin rights for the first week to set things up
Temporary admin rights break least privilege and are often forgotten.
Her access is reviewed at the end of the year
A review comes later. First she needs correct access to start.

q.q: An employee moves from Payroll to Marketing. Six months later he can still open payroll files. What went wrong?
o: His old access wasn't removed when his role changed
Right. Mover events should remove old access as well as add new access. Otherwise privilege creep builds up.
He was given a password that was far too short and easy to guess
A short password is a different weakness from leftover access.
Marketing should never have file access
Marketing needs its own files. The problem is the payroll access.
The payroll files weren't encrypted
Encryption doesn't stop an authorized account from opening files.

q.q: An employee is fired at 3:00 p.m. When should her accounts be disabled?
o: At or before the moment she's told
Right. Fast deprovisioning stops an upset former employee from taking or damaging data.
At the end of the week, when HR finishes the paperwork
Waiting leaves days for misuse.
When her manager remembers to ask IT
Deprovisioning should be triggered by the HR process, not by memory.
Only after her email has been archived
Archive first if needed, but disable her login right away.

q.q: Why do organizations run periodic access reviews?
o: To find and remove access people no longer need
Right. Reviews catch privilege creep, leftover accounts and mistakes.
To reset every user's password at the same time
Password resets are a separate control.
To give everyone a little more access each year
Reviews remove access. They don't add it.
To replace multifactor authentication
Reviews and MFA solve different problems.

q.q: A team sets up an AI bot that reads support tickets and updates the ticket system. How should its access be handled?
o: Give it its own service identity with only the access it needs, and review it like any account
Right. Bots and service accounts are identities too, and need an owner, least privilege and reviews.
Let it use the team lead's personal login
Sharing a person's login hides who did what and gives the bot too much access.
Give it domain admin rights so it never fails on a ticket it can't update
Admin rights for a bot create a huge target if it's misused.
Don't track it, because only humans need identities
Untracked bot accounts are a common way in for attackers.

q.q: During a quarterly review, the team finds 40 enabled accounts for people who left the company. What is the BEST fix for the root cause?
o: Link account deprovisioning to the HR offboarding process
Right. A trigger from HR removes access every time someone leaves, not just when a review catches it.
Delete the 40 accounts and move on
That fixes today's problem but not the gap that caused it.
Run access reviews every five years instead of every quarter
Reviewing less often would make this worse.
Require longer passwords for those accounts
Leftover accounts should be disabled, not hardened.

q.q: Which item is part of DEFINING ROLES in identity management?
o: Listing what access each job, like "payroll clerk", needs to do its work
Right. Role definitions are the template provisioning uses.
Choosing a font for the login page
Login page design isn't identity management.
Picking which antivirus to install
Antivirus choice isn't part of role definition.
Deciding how long the nightly backups are kept before deletion
Backup retention belongs to data management and DR.

q.q: A company wants one login, with MFA, for its email, HR app and cloud storage. Which identity tool fits BEST?
o: Single sign-on (SSO) through a central identity provider
Right. SSO lets one strong login, with MFA, unlock many apps and makes it easy to disable a user in one place.
A shared password for every app
Shared passwords remove accountability.
A separate local account in each app, each with its own password
Separate accounts are harder to manage and to remove when someone leaves.
A firewall rule for each app
Firewalls control network traffic, not who a user is.

q.q: An identity system flags that a user logged in from Ohio and, 20 minutes later, from Singapore. What is this check called?
o: Impossible travel detection
Right. No one can travel that far that fast, so one of the logins is probably an attacker.
Separation of duties
SoD splits tasks between people.
Mandatory access control
MAC is an access control model based on labels.
Deprovisioning
Deprovisioning removes access when someone leaves.

q.q: What is the MAIN risk of a shared account that a whole team uses?
o: Nobody can tell which person did what
Right. Shared accounts break accountability, and logs can't tie actions to one person.
Shared accounts can't use passwords
They can. The problem is accountability.
Shared accounts make the network slower
Account type doesn't affect network speed.
Shared accounts are always admin accounts
They aren't always admins, but they still hide who acted.

q.q: A contractor needs access for a 90-day project. Which approach is BEST?
o: An account that expires automatically at the end of the 90 days
Right. Built-in expiry makes sure the access ends even if nobody remembers.
A normal account, to be removed when someone notices the project is over
Relying on memory leaves old contractor accounts behind.
Letting the contractor use an employee's account
Sharing accounts breaks accountability and policy.
Full admin access so the contractor isn't slowed down
Contractors should get only what the project needs.

q.q: A login system starts asking for an extra check when a user signs in from a new device at 3 a.m., but not during normal workday logins. What is this?
o: Risk-based authentication
Right. The system looks at context, like device and time, and asks for more proof when risk is higher.
Single-factor authentication
The extra check means it isn't single-factor.
Discretionary access control (DAC)
DAC is about owners granting permissions on their files.
Account deprovisioning
Nothing is being removed here.

q.q: A help desk technician needs to reset passwords. Which access follows the principle of least privilege?
o: Rights to reset passwords, nothing more
Right. Least privilege grants only what the job needs.
Domain admin, so he never has to ask for more
Admin rights go far beyond resetting passwords.
Read access to every file share, just in case
"Just in case" access is exactly what least privilege removes.
The same rights as the IT manager
His manager's job is different, so the access should be too.

q.q: The person who creates a new vendor in the payment system shouldn't be the same person who approves payments to that vendor. Which principle is this?
o: Separation of duties
Right. Splitting the steps means one person can't commit fraud alone.
Least privilege
Least privilege limits access. SoD splits a process between people.
Need to know
Need to know limits what information someone sees.
Defense in depth (layering)
Defense in depth layers many controls.

q.q: In which access control model does the OWNER of a file decide who else can open it?
o: Discretionary access control (DAC)
Right. In DAC, owners grant permissions as they choose, like sharing a folder.
Mandatory access control (MAC)
In MAC, the system enforces labels and owners can't override them.
Role-based access control (RBAC)
RBAC grants access by job role, not by the owner's choice.
Rule-based access control
Rule-based uses system-wide rules, like time-of-day limits.

q.q: A military system lets a user with a Secret clearance read files labeled Secret and below, but never Top Secret, and users can't change the labels. Which model is this?
o: Mandatory access control (MAC)
Right. The system enforces labels and clearances. Users can't override them.
Discretionary access control (DAC)
In DAC, owners could change who has access.
Role-based access control (RBAC)
RBAC is based on job roles, not on classification labels.
Attribute-based access control (ABAC)
ABAC uses many attributes in policies. This scenario is classic label-based MAC.

q.q: A hospital gives every nurse the same set of permissions through a "Nurse" group, and new nurses are simply added to it. Which model is this?
o: Role-based access control (RBAC)
Right. Permissions are tied to the role, and people get them by being assigned to that role.
Discretionary access control (DAC)
Nobody is granting access file by file as an owner.
Mandatory access control (MAC)
There are no classification labels or clearances here.
Rule-based access control
Access comes from the role, not from a system-wide rule.

q.q: A badge only works at the office between 6 a.m. and 8 p.m. on weekdays, for everyone. Which kind of access control is this?
o: Rule-based access control
Right. A system-wide rule, here a time window, applies to every user.
Discretionary access control
The owner of a resource isn't choosing who gets in.
Role-based access control
The rule applies to everyone, whatever their role.
Mandatory access control
No sensitivity labels are involved.

q.q: An automated script copies files to a backup server every night. Which access fits least privilege?
o: Read on the source folder, write on the backup folder
Right. That's exactly what the job needs, and nothing more.
Full admin on both servers so it never breaks
Admin rights give an attacker who takes over the script full control.
The backup admin's personal login
Scripts should use their own identity, not a person's login.
Write access to every server, in case new folders appear somewhere later
Broad write access is a big risk if the script is misused.

q.q: Why is it a good idea for system admins to have two accounts: a normal one for email and web, and a separate admin one?
o: A phishing click won't run with admin rights
Right. Day-to-day work happens with low privilege, which limits the damage from a mistake.
It lets admins share their admin account with coworkers when they're away
Admin accounts should never be shared.
Two accounts mean admins don't need MFA
Both accounts still need strong authentication.
It doubles the number of licenses, which auditors like
Auditors care about risk, not license counts.

q.q: An employee only needs to see the customers in her region, but the app shows every customer nationwide. Which principle is being broken?
o: Need to know
Right. She should only see the information her work requires.
Separation of duties
SoD splits steps of a process. This is about too much visible data.
Non-repudiation
Non-repudiation is about proving who did something.
Availability
The data is available. Too much of it is visible.

q.q: A company lets an AI assistant answer staff questions using the company's file shares. Which control MOST protects confidential files?
o: It only returns files the user can already open
Right. Applying each user's permissions keeps the AI from becoming a way around access control.
The assistant gets read access to every share so its answers are complete
Then any user could get confidential data by asking the right question.
Staff promise not to ask about confidential topics
A promise isn't a control.
The assistant's answers are written in bold
Formatting doesn't protect anything.

q.q: What is the main benefit of reviewing who is in powerful groups, like Domain Admins, more often than normal groups?
o: Those accounts can do the most damage
Right. Privileged access deserves closer, more frequent review.
Normal groups never change
Normal groups change too, but they carry less risk.
Admins don't use passwords
Admins authenticate like anyone else.
It replaces the need for logging every admin action in the SIEM
Reviews and logging work together.

q.q: At which OSI layer do IP addresses and routers work?
o: Layer 3, Network
Right. The Network layer handles logical addressing (IP) and routing between networks.
Layer 2, Data Link
Layer 2 uses MAC addresses and switches inside one network.
Layer 4, Transport
Layer 4 handles TCP and UDP ports and delivery between hosts.
Layer 7, Application
Layer 7 is where apps like HTTP and DNS work.

q.q: Which protocol and port should replace Telnet for remote administration of a switch?
o: SSH on TCP 22
Right. SSH encrypts the session, including the password.
HTTP on TCP 80
HTTP isn't encrypted and isn't a remote shell.
FTP on TCP 21
FTP transfers files in clear text.
SNMP on UDP 161
SNMP is for monitoring, and older versions send community strings in clear text.

q.q: A remote worker connects to the office over hotel Wi-Fi. Which tool BEST protects the traffic between her laptop and the office?
o: A VPN that encrypts the whole connection
Right. A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel across the untrusted network.
A stronger screen lock password
A screen lock protects the device, not the traffic.
Turning off the laptop's Bluetooth and file sharing
Bluetooth isn't the path her traffic takes.
Using IPv6 instead of IPv4
IPv6 by itself doesn't encrypt traffic.

q.q: What is a key difference between IPv4 and IPv6 addresses?
o: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses and IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses
Right. IPv6's much larger space removes the address shortage.
IPv6 addresses are always written in dotted decimal, like IPv4
IPv6 is written in hexadecimal with colons.
IPv4 can't be routed across the internet
IPv4 is routed across the internet every day.
IPv6 has no addresses for local networks
IPv6 has link-local and unique local addresses.

q.q: A firewall rule allows TCP 443 inbound to the web server and blocks everything else. What is this rule doing?
o: Allowing HTTPS to the web server and denying all other traffic by default
Right. 443 is HTTPS, and "deny everything else" is the safe default.
Allowing remote desktop connections to the web server
RDP uses TCP 3389.
Allowing email to reach the web server
SMTP uses TCP 25.
Allowing DNS lookups from the web server
DNS uses port 53.

q.q: A next-generation firewall can block a specific app, like a file-sharing service, even when it uses port 443. What makes this possible?
o: It inspects the application layer
Right. Application awareness identifies the app regardless of the port it uses.
It only looks at source IP addresses
IP filtering can't tell which app is in the traffic.
It blocks every connection that uses port 443 by default
That would break all HTTPS websites.
It turns off encryption on the network
Firewalls don't turn off encryption for the network.

q.q: Which wireless setup is MOST secure for a small office?
o: WPA3 with a strong passphrase, or WPA3-Enterprise with individual logins
Right. WPA3 is the current standard. Enterprise mode gives each user their own credentials.
WEP with a 10-digit key
WEP can be cracked in minutes.
An open network with a hidden SSID
Hiding the name doesn't encrypt anything, and the SSID is easy to find.
WPA2 with the router's default password printed on the label
Default passwords are published online.

q.q: A factory's industrial control system (ICS) runs equipment that can't be offline even for a few minutes. Why is it hard to secure with normal IT practices?
o: Patching or rebooting can stop production
Right. ICS puts availability and safety first, so routine patching and scans need careful planning.
ICS devices never connect to any network
Many ICS networks are connected, which is part of the risk.
ICS systems are always brand new and fully patched by the vendor
They often run for decades on old software.
Encryption is illegal on ICS networks
It isn't illegal, but older devices may not support it.

q.q: A company buys smart thermostats and cameras for its offices. What is the BEST first step to reduce their risk?
o: Change default passwords and isolate them
Right. IoT devices often ship with weak defaults, and isolating them limits what an attacker can reach.
Connect them to the same network as the finance servers
That gives a hacked camera a path to finance.
Leave the default settings, since they came from a trusted brand
Default settings are often the weakest point.
Turn off the office firewall so the devices work smoothly
Removing the firewall exposes everything.

q.q: A company places its public web server in a separate zone between the internet and the internal network. What is this zone called?
o: A DMZ
Right. A DMZ holds public-facing services so attackers who break in don't land on the internal network.
A VLAN trunk
A trunk carries several VLANs between switches.
An intranet
An intranet is the internal network itself.
A honeypot network
A honeypot is a decoy built to attract attackers.

q.q: Which statement BEST describes zero trust?
o: Never trust a request just because it comes from inside the network; verify every one
Right. Zero trust checks identity, device and context for each access, wherever it comes from.
Trust anyone who is connected to the office network or the VPN
That's the old perimeter model zero trust replaces.
Block all users from every system
Zero trust grants access after verification. It doesn't block everyone.
Remove all firewalls and rely only on passwords
Zero trust uses many controls, not just passwords.

q.q: A company has a firewall, antivirus, MFA, backups and staff training. If one control fails, the others still help. What is this approach called?
o: Defense in depth
Right. Layered controls mean no single failure exposes everything.
Least privilege
Least privilege limits each user's access.
Separation of duties
SoD splits tasks between people.
Single point of failure
That's the opposite: one weak spot that brings everything down.

q.q: The network team puts printers, guest Wi-Fi and staff PCs on different VLANs. What is the MAIN security benefit?
o: A device hacked in one VLAN can't easily reach the others
Right. Segmentation limits how far an attacker can move.
The network uses less electricity
VLANs don't change power use in a meaningful way.
Users no longer need passwords
Segmentation doesn't replace authentication.
Every device on the network gets a faster internet connection
VLANs are about separation, not speed.

q.q: In a data center, each workload has its own firewall rules, so even two servers on the same subnet can only talk if a rule allows it. What is this?
o: Microsegmentation
Right. It enforces policy between individual workloads, not just between big zones.
Port forwarding
Port forwarding sends outside traffic to an inside host.
Network address translation
NAT rewrites addresses. It doesn't control which workloads can talk.
A flat network
A flat network has no segmentation at all.

q.q: A team trains AI models on copies of customer data. Where should the training environment sit?
o: In its own segment, separated from production systems, with only approved data flows
Right. Isolating the training environment limits what a breach there can reach.
On the same network as the production database, so data loads faster
Speed isn't worth giving a breach a direct path to production.
On a public cloud bucket that anyone with the link can read
A public bucket exposes the customer data.
On each data scientist's personal laptop
That spreads sensitive data onto devices the company can't fully control.

q.q: An attacker phishes one employee and then tries to reach the HR database. Under zero trust, what MOST likely stops him?
o: Every request to the database is checked against the user's role, device health and context
Right. Being inside the network isn't enough. Each access is verified.
Nothing, since the attacker is now inside the network and therefore trusted
That's exactly the assumption zero trust removes.
The firewall at the internet edge
He's already past the edge by using the employee's session.
The antivirus on the HR server
Antivirus may not see someone logging in with stolen access.

q.q: Which design creates a SINGLE POINT OF FAILURE?
o: All traffic goes through one firewall
Right. If that one firewall fails, the whole office loses connectivity.
Two firewalls in a failover pair
A failover pair removes the single point.
Two internet links from two different service providers
Two links add redundancy.
Servers spread across two data centers
Spreading servers out removes a single point.

q.q: Why might an organization use an AI-based intrusion detection system as well as signature-based detection?
o: It can flag new, unusual behavior
Right. Behavior-based detection can catch new attacks that have no signature yet.
It never gives false alarms
AI detectors still give false positives and need tuning.
It removes the need for a firewall at the network edge
Detection doesn't replace prevention controls.
It works without any network data
It needs traffic or logs to learn from and analyze.

q.q: A company rents virtual machines from a cloud provider and installs its own operating system and apps. Which service model is this?
o: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
Right. In IaaS the provider runs the hardware. The customer manages the OS and up.
Software as a Service (SaaS)
In SaaS the customer just uses a finished app.
Platform as a Service (PaaS)
In PaaS the provider also manages the OS and runtime.
Function as a Service (FaaS)
In FaaS you upload code and the provider runs everything under it.

q.q: Under the shared responsibility model, which task is ALWAYS the customer's job, whatever the cloud service model?
o: Managing who has access to its data and accounts
Right. Identities, access and the data itself always stay with the customer.
Replacing failed hard drives in the provider's data center
The provider handles physical hardware.
Guarding the data center doors
Physical security belongs to the provider.
Patching the hypervisor
The provider runs and patches the virtualization layer.

q.q: An online store's site automatically adds servers during a holiday sale and removes them afterward. Which cloud characteristic is this?
o: Rapid elasticity
Right. Resources grow and shrink quickly to match demand.
Measured service
Measured service means you pay for what you use.
Resource pooling
Pooling means many customers share the provider's hardware.
Broad network access
That means services can be reached from many kinds of devices over the network.

q.q: Many companies' workloads run on the same physical servers at a cloud provider, kept apart by software. Which characteristic is this, and what does it mean for security?
o: Resource pooling, so strong separation between customers is essential
Right. Shared hardware means the provider's isolation must keep one customer from reaching another.
Measured service, so customers must track their own bills
Billing is measured service, and it isn't the security point here.
On-demand self-service, so no one can create resources without a ticket
Self-service means customers create resources themselves, without a ticket.
Rapid elasticity, so every server is physically separate
Elasticity is about scaling, and pooled servers aren't separate.

q.q: A team creates new cloud servers itself through a web portal, without calling the provider. Which characteristic is this?
o: On-demand self-service
Right. Customers provision resources themselves, when they need them.
Rapid elasticity
Elasticity is about scaling quickly, not who does the provisioning.
Measured service
Measured service is about metering and billing.
Resource pooling
Pooling is about shared hardware.

q.q: A government agency wants cloud services that only other government agencies share. Which deployment model fits?
o: Community cloud
Right. A community cloud is shared by organizations with common needs, like government rules.
Public cloud
Public cloud is open to any customer.
Private cloud
Private cloud serves one organization only.
Hybrid cloud
Hybrid cloud mixes two or more models. It doesn't describe who shares it.

q.q: A company stores files in a cloud storage bucket and leaves it open to the public by mistake. Under shared responsibility, who is at fault?
o: The customer, because it controls the bucket's access settings
Right. The provider offers the settings, but configuring access is the customer's job.
The cloud provider, because it owns and runs the storage hardware
The provider secures the platform, not each customer's settings.
Nobody, because cloud data is always public
Cloud data is private unless someone makes it public.
The internet service provider
The ISP has nothing to do with bucket settings.

q.q: A company uses a hosted AI service through the provider's website. Which security task stays with the company?
o: Deciding what data staff may send to it
Right. Even in SaaS, the customer controls its data and its users.
Patching the servers and GPUs the AI model runs on
In SaaS, the provider patches its own servers.
Cooling the provider's data center
Facilities belong to the provider.
Writing the AI model's code
The provider builds and runs the model.

q.q: A business mainly wants to stop managing servers and just use email and office apps over the web. Which model fits BEST?
o: Software as a Service (SaaS)
Right. SaaS delivers a finished app, and the provider runs everything under it.
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
With IaaS the business would still manage servers.
An on-premises data center
That means running servers in-house.
A private cloud the business builds itself
Building a private cloud means more server work, not less.

q.q: A company replaces all but the last four digits of credit card numbers with X's on its support screens. What is this called?
o: Data masking
Right. Masking hides part of the data so staff see only what they need.
Hashing
A hash replaces the whole value with a fixed-length digest and can't be read back.
Data sanitization
Sanitization destroys data on media before disposal.
Symmetric encryption
Encryption scrambles the whole value and needs a key to read it.

q.q: Two offices need to send large files to each other quickly and securely. They already share a secret key safely. Which encryption type fits BEST?
o: Symmetric encryption, like AES
Right. One shared key encrypts and decrypts, and it's fast for large data.
Asymmetric encryption, like RSA, for the whole file
Asymmetric encryption is much slower. It's mostly used to exchange keys or sign.
Hashing the files with SHA-256
Hashing checks integrity. It doesn't hide the content.
Masking the files
Masking hides parts of data on a screen. It doesn't protect files in transit.

q.q: Before giving old laptops to a recycler, what should a company do with their drives?
o: Sanitize them with an approved wipe, or destroy them, and keep a record
Right. Sanitization makes the data unrecoverable, and the record proves it was done.
Delete all the user files and then empty the recycle bin
Deleted files can usually be recovered.
Quick-format the drives
A quick format leaves most data recoverable.
Remove the stickers with the asset tags
Removing labels doesn't touch the data.

q.q: A file is labeled CONFIDENTIAL. What does the label mainly do?
o: Shows how the file must be handled
Right. Labels make the classification visible so the right handling rules apply.
Encrypts the file automatically when it's saved
A label on its own doesn't encrypt anything.
Deletes the file after 30 days
Retention is a separate rule.
Proves who created the file
Labels show sensitivity, not authorship.

q.q: Security leaders worry that future quantum computers could break RSA. What should they plan for?
o: Moving to quantum-resistant (post-quantum) algorithms
Right. Post-quantum algorithms are designed to resist attacks from quantum computers.
Using shorter RSA keys so they're faster to replace
Shorter keys are weaker against every attacker.
Stopping all encryption until quantum computers exist
That would expose data right now.
Replacing encryption with hashing everywhere
Hashing can't replace encryption, because you can't read data back from a hash.

q.q: A SIEM receives 5,000 alerts a day, and analysts are missing real attacks. Which change helps MOST?
o: Tune and correlate alerts so related events become one prioritized case
Right. Correlation and tuning cut noise so the serious events stand out.
Turn off logging on the busiest servers
Less logging means less visibility, not better detection.
Have analysts close every alert older than one hour to keep up
Closing alerts without looking at them hides real attacks.
Send every alert to the CEO
Leadership can't triage thousands of alerts.

q.q: Which event should an analyst triage FIRST?
o: An admin account logging in from an unknown country, then turning off logging
Right. A privileged account plus an attempt to hide activity points to a likely active compromise.
A firewall blocking a port scan from the internet
Blocked scans are routine. The control worked.
A user locking themselves out after three wrong passwords in a row
Usually a forgotten password. It's low priority on its own.
An antivirus update finishing on 200 PCs
That's normal maintenance.

q.q: A group breaks into a company's network to steal its product designs for a foreign government. Which threat actor type is this MOST likely?
o: A nation-state actor
Right. Spying for a government to steal secrets is a classic nation-state motive.
A hacktivist
Hacktivists attack to make a political or social point, often publicly.
A script kiddie
Script kiddies use ready-made tools and rarely run long, targeted spy operations.
A careless insider
A careless insider causes harm by accident, not as a planned operation.

q.q: A threat intelligence feed reports that a new ransomware gang uses a specific IP address and file hash. How should a SOC use this?
o: Hunt for the indicators and add detections
Right. Indicators of compromise from threat intel help find and block known attacker activity.
Ignore it, because intel feeds are only for large companies
Organizations of every size can use threat intel.
Post the indicators on the company website
Publishing them doesn't protect the company.
Shut down every server until the gang is caught
That's an overreaction that stops the business.

q.q: Analysts map an attacker's steps to tactics like initial access, persistence and exfiltration so they can spot gaps in detection. Which framework is this?
o: MITRE ATT&CK
Right. ATT&CK catalogs real attacker tactics and techniques.
The OSI model
OSI describes network layers, not attacker behavior.
ISO/IEC 27001
ISO 27001 is a standard for running a security management program.
The CIA triad
The CIA triad names security goals, not attacker steps.

q.q: An analyst confirms malware on one workstation that is trying to spread. What should happen NEXT?
o: Contain it by isolating the workstation
Right. Containment stops the spread before eradication and recovery.
Reimage the workstation right away without saving anything
Wiping first can destroy evidence the team needs.
Write the lessons-learned report
Lessons learned comes after recovery.
Email every employee the malware file so they can recognize it
Spreading the malware file is dangerous.

q.q: A company's incident response team talks through a fake ransomware scenario in a conference room, without touching any systems. What kind of exercise is this?
o: A tabletop exercise
Right. Tabletops walk through the plan by discussion, which is a low-cost way to find gaps.
A full-interruption test
That would actually shut systems down and fail over.
A penetration test
A pentest actively attacks systems.
A vulnerability scan
A scan checks systems for known weaknesses.

q.q: During an incident, a manager wants to post details on social media right away. According to a good incident response plan, who should approve public statements?
o: The communications or legal team named in the plan
Right. The plan names who speaks for the organization, so messages are accurate and lawful.
Any employee who knows what happened
Uncoordinated posts can spread wrong information or break legal rules.
The attacker, to confirm the details
Never coordinate public statements with the attacker.
The help desk, since it takes the calls from customers
The help desk follows the plan, but it doesn't approve public statements.

q.q: An incident response plan says evidence must be handled with a chain of custody. Why?
o: To prove the evidence wasn't altered
Right. Chain of custody records who handled the evidence and when.
To make the investigation go faster
It adds steps. Its value is that the evidence stays trustworthy.
To let anyone on the team edit the evidence
The point is to prevent unrecorded changes.
To delete the evidence once the incident is closed out
Chain of custody is about keeping evidence, not deleting it.

q.q: After a breach is fully recovered, the team meets to discuss what went well and what to change. Why is this step important?
o: It improves the plan and controls
Right. Lessons learned turns the incident into fixes.
It decides which employee to blame
Good reviews focus on process, not blame.
It's only required for incidents that cost over $1 million
Every significant incident deserves a review.
It replaces the need to test the plan
Testing is still needed. Reviews and tests support each other.

q.q: A company still runs a server on an operating system the vendor no longer patches. What is the BEST long-term action?
o: Plan to replace or upgrade it, and isolate it until then
Right. End-of-life software won't get security fixes, so it must be retired, with compensating controls meanwhile.
Keep it, because it still works
Working isn't the same as being safe. New flaws will never be fixed.
Install a newer antivirus product on it and keep it running
Antivirus can't fix unpatched OS flaws.
Hide it from the asset inventory
Hiding an asset makes it riskier, not safer.

q.q: Why does a company need an accurate asset inventory?
o: You can't protect what you don't know about
Right. The inventory is the starting point for every other control.
It replaces the need for a firewall
An inventory doesn't block traffic.
It's only needed for tax purposes
Finance uses it too, but security depends on it.
It lets users install any software they like on their devices
An inventory is about tracking, not permission.

q.q: An admin changes a firewall rule on Friday night without approval, and Monday morning the payroll app can't reach its database. Which process would MOST likely have prevented this?
o: Change management, with review, approval, testing and a back-out plan
Right. A reviewed change would have caught the impact, or planned a quick rollback.
Data classification
Classification labels data. It doesn't control changes.
Security awareness training for admins
Training helps users, but this needed a change process.
Multifactor authentication
MFA proves identity. It doesn't review changes.

q.q: A team keeps a secure, approved settings template for every new server and checks servers against it each month. What is the template called?
o: A configuration baseline
Right. A baseline is the approved secure setup that systems are checked against.
A risk register
A risk register tracks risks.
A business impact analysis
A BIA ranks business processes for continuity.
An incident playbook
A playbook gives response steps for a type of incident.

q.q: A company uses an AI tool from a vendor that announces the tool will be retired next year. What should the asset life cycle process do?
o: Plan a replacement and how to remove the tool and its data before support ends
Right. Asset management covers the whole life cycle, including end of life for software and AI tools.
Keep using it after support ends, since it's already paid for
Unsupported tools stop getting security fixes.
Delete the tool tonight without a plan
An unplanned removal can break business processes and lose data.
Nothing, because AI tools aren't assets
Software and AI services are assets and need tracking.

q.q: One team attacks a company's systems the way a real attacker would while another team defends, and then they work together to improve detection. What is the joint effort called?
o: Purple teaming
Right. Purple teams combine red (attack) and blue (defense) to improve together.
Black-box testing
Black-box describes how much the tester knows, not teams working together.
A vulnerability scan
A scan is automated and doesn't involve attack and defense teams.
A tabletop exercise
A tabletop is a discussion, not a live attack.

q.q: Which test looks at an application's SOURCE CODE for flaws without running it?
o: Static analysis (SAST)
Right. Static analysis reviews code before it runs.
Dynamic analysis (DAST)
Dynamic analysis tests the running application.
A physical penetration test
Physical tests target buildings and people.
A load test
Load tests measure performance under heavy use.

q.q: A tester in a fake delivery uniform walks into the office behind an employee without badging in. What is he testing?
o: Physical security against tailgating
Right. Physical pentests check whether people and doors stop unauthorized entry.
The strength of the office Wi-Fi encryption
Walking in has nothing to do with Wi-Fi.
The application's input validation
That's application testing.
The backup restore process
That's DR testing.

q.q: Before writing code for a new app, the team lists what attackers might target and how, then designs defenses. What is this activity?
o: Threat modeling
Right. Threat modeling finds likely attacks early, when fixes are cheapest.
Penetration testing
Pentesting attacks a system that already exists.
Change management
Change management controls changes to running systems.
Data sanitization
Sanitization wipes data from media.

q.q: What is a key difference between a vulnerability scan and a penetration test?
o: A scan finds possible weaknesses; a pentest tries to exploit them to show the real impact
Right. Pentests go further, with permission, to prove what an attacker could actually do.
A scan always needs written permission, and a pentest never does
Both need authorization. A pentest needs especially clear written scope.
A pentest is fully automatic and a scan is done by hand
Scans are mostly automated. Pentests are mostly hands-on.
They are two names for the same test
They differ in depth and purpose.
